title: Ghost Ship
full_review:
Despite its spooky movie poster, "Ghost Ship" (Warner Bros.) is more ghastly than ghostly.

The opening scene mines new lows in showing massive, unexplained carnage as a steel wire on board a 1962 Italian luxury liner snaps, transecting the bodies of hundreds of tuxedoed and begowned passengers who soon collapse onto a floor of gore. This scene will be repeated, but in terms of narrative it doesn't make any more sense the second time around. By that point in the movie it's clear that what plot exists is simply to move the viewer from one killing scene to another; a satisfying explanation of events will never materialize.

Most of the action is set in the present day after bush pilot Jack (Desmond Harrington) offers to lead the five-man, one-woman salvage crew to the site of the long-lost ocean liner he spotted in the Bering Sea. As the "Antonia Graza" is adrift in international waters, the seven can claim it and all its contents as their own.

The close, plucky crew is forced to take Jack along in their tugboat and eventually the doomed liner looms large in the night before them. Exploring the empty ship, team leader Epps (Julianna Margulies) thinks for a moment she sees a little girl, the first of the ghosts who will appear to the crew, mostly to lure them to their doom.

Unnerved by strange occurrences, Capt. Murphy (Gabriel Byrne) gets the crew to agree to abandon tugging the ship back in favor of just absconding with cases of gold bullion found aboard. But loading it on the tugboat won't be a simple task with evil spirits bedeviling the crew's every move.

Some credit must be given to director Steve Beck for eerie visuals that carry the film for a while until the sloppiness of the preposterous script tries viewer patience. It's hard not to wonder with satellite communications why the huge liner hasn't been spotted in 40 years or what happened to all the skeletons that should be on board. The cockamamie explanation tendered about how the gold figures into all this is just an excuse to restage how scores of other passengers and crew were murdered. Greed is supposed to fuel this story in which the cycle of evil triumphant lives to attract new victims, but this theme is only lamely developed.

Lest sex be ignored alongside the violence and objectionable language that abounds, the first mate (Isaiah Washington), who can't wait to get home to marry his fiancee, is seen ready to bed a red-gowned siren who strips to the waist but has other ideas when he gets close. That fiancee had better dye her bridal gown black.

It is an uninspired horror flick with nothing special to recommend it, and one can only hope "Ghost Ship" will vanish without a trace.

Due to recurring violence with excessive gore, sexual innuendo with nudity, frequent profanity and much rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
